topComments.author: rramadass
topComments.text: This is one of my favourite Edgar Allan Poe stories. The cipher is just a simple monoalphabetic substitution based on frequency analysis. The same idea was "reused" by Arthur Conan Doyle in his story "The Adventure of the Dancing Men" where he used pictures of dancing men for his cipher text. Note that Conan Doyle indirectly acknowledged Poe's influence (via his character Auguste Dupin) on Sherlock Holmes in "A Study in Scarlet". Poe wrote three stories starring his detective Auguste Dupin all of which are fantastic. They are "The Murders in the Rue Morgue", "The Mystery of Marie Roget" and "The Purloined Letter". They are a must-read for all fans of detective fiction. Folks who have read Sherlock Holmes can see how much he was influenced by Dupin. The stories often have some close/clever observations/reasonings which given Poe's style of writing are a delight to read. For example the opening paragraph of "The Murders in the Rue Morgue" reads; THE mental features discoursed of as the analytical, are, in themselves, but little susceptible of analysis. We appreciate them only in their effects. We know of them, among other things, that they are always to their possessor, when inordinately possessed, a source of the liveliest enjoyment. As the strong man exults in his physical ability, delighting in such exercises as call his muscles into action, so glories the analyst in that moral activity which disentangles. He derives pleasure from even the most trivial occupations bringing his talent into play. He is fond of enigmas, of conundrums, of hieroglyphics; exhibiting in his solutions of each a degree of acumen which appears to the ordinary apprehension præternatural. His results, brought about by the very soul and essence of method, have, in truth, the whole air of intuition. The essence of why people love solving problems!

jobs.text: I’m Chris, VP Engineering at Fazeshift. We’re nine engineers plus our Founder/CTO and me, and I’m hiring someone who can help us do more, better: increase both what we can build and the quality and sophistication of the software we build. Accounts receivable sounds boring until you look under the hood. It sits at the intersection of money, business relationships, software systems of various vintages, and a huge amount of repetitive human work. Instead of giving finance teams another dashboard to stare at, we’re building AI agents that actually do the work across billing, collections, payments, cash application, and the systems connecting them. We’ve grown revenue 12x since 2024, and eight unicorns now run AR on Fazeshift. A big part of what makes the engineering interesting is that we’re intentionally not the system of record. Our customers already run on ERPs, CRMs, banks, billing systems, payment processors, spreadsheets, and internal software, so we have to understand state across systems we don’t control, act safely in them, and recover when reality disagrees with what an API says should have happened. A timeout doesn’t necessarily mean a write failed. Webhooks can arrive late or twice. A payment may not contain enough information to identify an invoice. In those cases, blindly retrying can be exactly the wrong thing to do. We use coding agents heavily ourselves. Engineers use Conductor, stacked PRs, Linear, and multiple frontier models every day, with internal skills and tooling that let agents drive and validate our local development environment. We’re especially interested in engineers whose development workflow has already materially changed because of coding agents: people who are comfortable delegating meaningful work, keeping independent threads moving in parallel, debugging where agents get stuck, and improving the surrounding system when the workflow breaks down. But generated code is still your code . Judgment, debugging, systems thinking, taste, and understanding what actually shipped matter more here, not less. Our development style is roughly: design enough to find the shape of the problem, then build to learn. There’s a short distance here between noticing a problem, deciding what should happen, building it, and seeing the result in production with our customers. You’ll own meaningful problems from ambiguity through design, implementation, rollout, and production, and you’ll work directly with the people affected by what you build. We’re looking for 5+ years of professional experience, strong TypeScript/full-stack skills, solid systems judgment, and real production ownership. No fintech background needed. Stack: TypeScript/Next.js, tRPC, Prisma/MySQL/PlanetScale, Inngest, AWS. I read every HN application myself. Email chris.zehner@fazeshift.com with HN in the subject, your LinkedIn/GitHub/résumé, and a few sentences about something interesting you’ve built or improved recently.

Fuzzy-matching the entry title against XMLTV display-name : too many false matches between similarly named entries. Parsing team names and start time out of the title with a regex: works until the playlist changes its title format. My question: For per-event entries, is it more robust to generate the XMLTV myself from a fixtures schedule (one <programme> per fixture) than to look for them in an existing XMLTV file? stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: I've found this post that explains how to create a new key with a forward slash. That works great if you create new keys, but renaming them doesn't seem to work. Suppose you have this registry key: HKLM:\SOFTWARE\MySoftware\Path=//Server/UNC/path/goes/here If you run thisE Rename-Item -Path "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\MySoftware\Path=//Server/UNC/path/goes/here" -NewName "Path=//Server/New/UNC/path/here" It will fail with Rename-Item : The registry key at the specified path does not exist. However, if the new name does not have any forward slash in it: Rename-Item -Path "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\MySoftware\Path=//Server/UNC/path/goes/here" -NewName "Path=no slash here" Then it runs fine. So it would seem that it is the -NewName that cannot use forward slashes. This post had a similar issue but with Get-ChildItem so it doesn't apply here (backtick doesn't work for the -NewName flag). Interestingly, both Copy-Item and Move-Item works even when -Destination has forward slashes in the path, so it seems to be limited to Rename-Item. How can I rename a registry key where the new name has forward slashes in the key name?

infoqArticles.description: Cloudflare has opened a closed beta of its OHTTP Gateway, a managed endpoint that decrypts Oblivious HTTP requests for an origin. The design choice drawing attention is a refusal: the Gateway will not decrypt requests arriving from Cloudflare Workers or from hosts proxied through Cloudflare, because that would put client identifiers and request contents in the same hands. By Steef-Jan Wiggers
infoqArticles.author: Steef-Jan Wiggers

infoqArticles.title: Spotify More Than Doubled Monthly Code Changes as AI Accelerated Development
infoqArticles.description: Spotify reports that AI-assisted development more than doubled monthly merged changes, prompting a review of quality and reliability controls across its engineering organization. The company describes changes to testing, observability, rollback capacity, workload prioritization, and automated maintenance as it adapts to higher software change volume. By Leela Kumili
infoqArticles.author: Leela Kumili

infoqArticles.title: Article: When Should You Use Liquid Clustering? Benchmarking Lakehouse Layout Strategies
infoqArticles.description: Physical data layout is one of the most consequential decisions in lakehouse engineering. The author compares Liquid Clustering, ZOrdering, and partitioning across four workload types on Delta Lake, uncovering two undocumented failure modes that likely affect production systems today and offering a decision framework for choosing the right layout strategy. By Kushal Kumar Vishwakarma
infoqArticles.author: Kushal Kumar Vishwakarma

infoqArticles.title: Podcast: What Does It Really Mean To Program With AI: A Conversation with Joy Ebertz
infoqArticles.description: In this podcast, Michael Stiefel spoke to Joy Ebertz about how the use of artificial intelligence is changing the way architects and developers do their jobs. Focusing on the long term success of the business is one of the most neglected tasks of an architect. This task becomes particularly important as the nature of artificial intelligence changes the landscape of software development. By Joy Ebe
infoqArticles.author: Joy Ebertz

infoqArticles.title: Presentation: You Can't Trust Your AI Bill. And Neither Can I
infoqArticles.description: Erik Peterson discusses why AI spend is eclipsing cloud bills, triggering a major software engineering cost crisis. He explains tokenmaxxing, unit economics, forced developer promotions, and why fully autonomous AI will write, deploy, and govern code by 2028. By Erik Peterson
infoqArticles.author: Erik Peterson
